title: Data processing agreement
intro: This data processing agreement (DPA) forms part of the agreement between {company} and the clinic that uses {product}. It sets out how we process personal data on the clinic's behalf, as required by Article 28 of the UK GDPR.

sections.heading: 1. Parties and roles
paragraphs: The clinic is the controller of the personal data it puts into {product}, including patient information. {company} ("we") is its processor.
This DPA applies for as long as we process personal data for the clinic, including after the agreement ends until the data is returned or deleted.

sections.heading: 2. Subject matter, nature and purpose
paragraphs: We process personal data only to provide {product} and its support to the clinic, as described in the terms and the clinic's order.
Categories of data subjects: the clinic's patients, its staff and users, and the referrers, insurers and other contacts the clinic records.
Categories of personal data: identification and contact details, appointment and billing details, and the health information the clinic records (special category data). Annex 1 gives more detail.

sections.heading: 3. Instructions
paragraphs: We process personal data only on the clinic's documented instructions – this DPA, the terms, the clinic's order and the clinic's use of the service's settings – unless the law requires otherwise, in which case we tell the clinic first unless the law forbids it.
We tell the clinic straight away if we think an instruction breaks data protection law.

sections.heading: 4. Confidentiality
paragraphs: Everyone we authorise to process the personal data is bound by a duty of confidentiality.

sections.heading: 5. Security
paragraphs: We take appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect the personal data, as set out in Annex 2 and on our security page. They include encryption in transit and at rest, two-step verification for every user, access limited by role and an audit trail.

sections.heading: 6. Sub-processors
paragraphs: The clinic gives us general authorisation to use sub-processors. The current list, with what each does, where it processes data and the safeguard for any transfer, is in Annex 3.

We tell the clinic at least 30 days before adding or replacing a sub-processor that handles the clinic's personal data, so the clinic can object. If the clinic objects on reasonable data protection grounds and we cannot resolve it, the clinic may end the affected service without penalty. Each sub-processor is bound by data protection terms no less protective than this DPA, and we remain responsible to the clinic for its work, within the limits in section 12.

sections.heading: 7. International transfers
paragraphs: Clinic data is stored in the UK (London). Where a sub-processor processes personal data outside the UK, the transfer is protected by an adequacy regulation, the UK Extension to the EU-US Data Privacy Framework or the International Data Transfer Addendum, as Annex 3 records.

sections.heading: 8. Helping the clinic
paragraphs: We help the clinic, taking into account the nature of the processing, to answer requests from people exercising their rights, and with security, breach notification, data protection impact assessments and consultation with the Information Commissioner's Office.

sections.heading: 9. Personal data breaches
paragraphs: We tell the clinic without undue delay, and in any case within 48 hours, after becoming aware of a personal data breach affecting its data, with the information the clinic needs to meet its own obligations. Where not all the information is available at once, we give it in stages as we learn it.
Telling the clinic about a breach, or helping it respond, is not an admission of fault or liability.

sections.heading: 10. Return and deletion
paragraphs: When the agreement ends, the clinic can export its data. We then delete it within 30 days, unless the law requires us to keep it, and confirm the deletion in writing on request.

If a free trial ends without a paid plan, the clinic's data is kept read-only for 90 days after the trial ends, so that the clinic can choose a plan or export its data. We email the clinic at least 14 days before the deletion, and then delete the data.
Copies in our backups are not restored or used, and are overwritten as the backups expire on their normal cycle (currently 7 days).

sections.heading: 11. Information and audits
paragraphs: We make available the information needed to show that we meet these obligations: our security measures, sub-processor list, policies and any certificates we hold, and written answers to a reasonable security questionnaire.

If that information is not enough, the clinic, or an independent auditor it appoints who is bound by confidentiality, may carry out a reasonable audit at most once a year, on at least 30 days' written notice, during business hours and at the clinic's own cost. More than once a year is allowed only after a personal data breach affecting the clinic's data or where a regulator requires it.

sections.heading: 12. Liability
paragraphs: Each party's total liability under or in connection with this DPA and the terms, including for data protection claims, is limited to £600 in total. Neither party is liable for loss of profits, revenue, business or goodwill, or for any indirect or consequential loss.

We are not liable for any loss caused by the clinic, its users or its instructions, including the use of the clinic's sign-in details or devices, personal data the clinic sends to the wrong person or shares outside the service, or the clinic's own systems.

Any claim must be notified to the other party in writing within 3 months of the claiming party becoming aware of the event giving rise to it, with reasonable detail. A claim not notified in that time cannot be brought.
Nothing in this DPA limits liability that cannot be limited by law, or the rights of individuals or the powers of the Information Commissioner's Office.

sections.heading: 13. General
paragraphs: If this DPA and the terms conflict, this DPA wins on anything about personal data. This DPA is governed by the law of England and Wales.

The clinic accepts this DPA online when it signs up, or by signing a copy before its account is set up. For online acceptance, the version accepted, who accepted it and when are recorded with the clinic's account; a signed copy is kept for as long as the agreement lasts and for 6 years after.

sections.heading: Annex 1 – Details of the processing
paragraphs: Duration: the term of the agreement and the return and deletion period after it.
Frequency: continuous, while the clinic uses the service.
Retention: as the clinic sets it in the service, and as section 10 says at the end.

sections.heading: Annex 2 – Security measures
paragraphs: Hosting: the service and its database run in UK data centres in London.
Encryption: TLS 1.2 or later in transit; AES-256 at rest, with patient files and notes also encrypted with a separate key for each clinic.
Access: invite-only accounts, two-step verification for every user, and access set by role and by site.
Audit trail: every sign-in, view, change and signature is recorded and cannot be edited; audit records are kept for 8 years.
Records: clinical notes lock when signed; amendments are tracked and the original is kept.
Backups: daily, kept for 7 days, stored in the UK.
Minimisation: when a clinic switches on drafting from notes, only a minimised extract is sent – no patient name, date of birth, address or contact details.
Retention: the clinic sets how long reports are kept and they are deleted automatically; a clinic's data is deleted after it leaves as section 10 says.
Incidents: security issues are acknowledged within one working day and breaches reported as section 9 says.
Organisation: confidentiality duties for everyone with access, written access-control and incident policies, and registration with the Information Commissioner's Office (ZC135044).

sections.heading: Annex 3 – Sub-processors
paragraphs: Vercel Inc. – application hosting. Runs in London (UK); the company is in the US. Safeguard for any access from outside the UK: the UK Extension to the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, with the EU standard contractual clauses and the UK Addendum as a fallback.

Supabase Inc. – database and patient file storage. Stored in London (UK). Safeguard for any access from outside the UK: the EU standard contractual clauses with the UK International Data Transfer Addendum.

MailerSend, Inc. – sending service emails such as invitations, sign-in links and notifications. Stored in the EU (Belgium); the company is in the US and may access data from there. Safeguard: the EU standard contractual clauses with the UK Addendum.

Stripe Payments UK Ltd – subscription billing and, where the clinic switches it on, card payments from patients. UK, EU and US. Safeguard: the UK Extension to the EU-US Data Privacy Framework or the International Data Transfer Addendum.
The SMS Works Ltd – text messages to patients, where the clinic switches them on. UK.
PostHog Inc. – usage statistics, only after consent. EU cloud (Germany). Safeguard: UK adequacy regulation for the EU.

Cloudflare Inc. – the human check on public booking and patient sign-in, where switched on. Global network; the check keeps no personal data afterwards. Safeguard: the UK Extension to the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, with the EU standard contractual clauses as a fallback.

Anthropic PBC – the drafting service, only where the clinic switches drafting from notes on. US. It receives only the minimised extract in Annex 2 and does not use it to train its models. It deletes it within 30 days, unless the law requires otherwise or the content is flagged under its usage policy (then kept for up to 2 years). Safeguard: the EU standard contractual clauses with the UK International Data Transfer Addendum.
